title: How antimalarial drugs act on the blood-stage parasite
ariaLabel: Schematic of the malaria parasite in a red cell: it digests haemoglobin and must turn toxic haem into inert haemozoin, it must make folate, and artemisinins generate damaging free radicals with the help of haem iron. Chloroquine-type drugs block haem detoxification, antifolates block folate synthesis, and artemisinins increase radical damage.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: Haemoglobin digested
nodes.info: The parasite digests the red cell's haemoglobin for amino acids. This releases haem, which is toxic to it.

nodes.label: Haem made safe
nodes.info: Haem polymerised to haemozoin. When this step is blocked, free haem accumulates and damages the parasite.

nodes.label: Folate precursors
nodes.info: The parasite makes its own folate from precursors, unlike humans who take it in the diet.

nodes.label: Folate made
nodes.info: Folate is needed for the parasite's DNA building and growth.

nodes.label: Haem iron
nodes.info: Iron from haem inside the parasite.

nodes.label: Radical damage
nodes.info: Free radical damage to parasite proteins. More damage means less parasite.

nodes.label: Parasites in the blood
nodes.info: A teaching score for the parasite load in the blood: growth needs safe haem and folate, and radical damage lowers it.

edges.label: haem polymerase
edges.info: The parasite turns toxic free haem into inert haemozoin (malaria pigment). Chloroquine-type drugs block this, so toxic haem builds up and kills the parasite.
This adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: folate synthesis
edges.info: DHPS and DHFR enzymes of the parasite folate pathway. Antifolates block them, so DNA building stops.
This adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: radical formation
edges.info: Artemisinins are activated by haem iron and form damaging free radicals that attack parasite proteins. A rise in this step means more damage.
More radical damage means fewer parasites.

sources: Where each class acts. Chloroquine-type drugs block haem polymerisation, antifolates block folate synthesis, and artemisinins generate free-radical damage activated by haem iron. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Primaquine and tafenoquine (liver stages, G6PD), atovaquone, quinine, resistance, species differences, severe malaria, pregnancy, adverse effects and prevention are left out. Parasite load is drawn as a teaching score. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
